newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania fuel rises may push inflation over 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: Romania fuel rises may push inflation over 10 pct.

text.p: Romania's doubling of fuel prices to meet International Monetary Fund recommendations was a positive step but could push monthly inflation to 10 percent this month, a prominent analyst said on Wednesday.
"There is no doubt that increasing fuel prices benefits the reforms," economist Ilie Serbanescu said by telephone.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's reformist government, in power since the defeat of ex-communists in November elections, doubled petrol prices starting January 1 to help cover losses caused by the depreciating leu currency.
A litre of premium rose to 1,900 lei (46 cents) per litre from 990, but remains much lower than prices in western Europe.

The increase triggered a chain reaction on a wide range of goods, with rises in staples like milk and meat cutting deeper into the budgets of consumers battered by post-Communist economic change. Average monthly wages stand at the equivalent of about $100, far behind ex-Communist Poland and Hungary.

Newspapers accused shops of blatant profiteering by raising prices without any justification. Statistics show Romanians' purchasing power now stands at 72 percent of 1990 levels, a year after Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was ousted.

"I don't rule out 10 percent inflation this month," Serbanescu said. "We are witnessing a tide of high prices with no connection to increases in fuel prices. There are many using this opportunity to turn a quick profit."
Year-on-year inflation last November stood at 47.4 percent, well above a 20 percent target agreed with the IMF.
An overall economic plan produced by the government in the aftermath of the election contained few figures and gave no forecast for 1997 inflation.
An IMF mission is to arrive in Bucharest this month to discuss a new loan accord with Ciorbea's government.
The Fund last year suspended a $460 million accord on grounds that the former leftist government had missed targets, including bringing fuel prices gradually up to world levels.
"Romania is crossing a period when all macro-economic balances have changed. It is hard to predict when they are going to be again on the right track," Serbanescu said.
He added that it was vital that electricity and heating prices should also be increased to avoid "two waves of price increases, instead of one".
"The government should act as quickly as possible. Failure to do so would complicate reforms, expose the cabinet to pressure from trade unions and generate higher inflation."
Both the state-run Renel RA electricity and Radet RA thermal power utilities said last month they were considering plans to raise tariffs but gave no deadline.
Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara told the daily Cronica Romana that the government would compensate consumers for new energy prices by cutting income tax for low wage-earners.
But he said the government would avoid inflationary steps like wage indexations or cash handouts.

The leu has fallen steadily in value over the past year and is now quoted at 4,200 on the interbank market, where market restrictions keep its rate artificially high. A dollar at Bucharest exchange shops fetches about 5,600 lei.
